title: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
hook: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tukaram sank his notebooks in the Indrayani and sat on the bank until, tradition says, they rose. What did you stop defending? Day nine hundred twenty-one.

Before dawn, on the stone steps that run down to the Ganges at Kashi, a young weaver lies stretched across a step in the dark. He knows a famous teacher, Ramananda, comes down these steps to bathe at this hour. The teacher's foot comes down on him in the dark. Startled, Ramananda cries out the name of God: Ram, Ram. And the young man gets up and goes home, holding those words as if they'd been handed to him on purpose. That, tradition says, is how Kabir got his teacher.
screen: `STEPS DOWN TO THE GANGES.` → `A FOOT IN THE DARK.` → `RAM, RAM.`

segments.voice: Kabir is remembered as a weaver in Kashi, working a loom, raised, tradition says, by a Muslim weaver couple, Niru and Nima, who found him as a baby by a pond. A man between worlds, who spent his life making cloth and making songs. And he left a particular kind of song: the doha. A doha is a couplet, two lines that rhyme, short enough to remember after hearing it once, sharp enough to keep working on you afterward. Kabir's dohas are passed along by people singing them and quoting them. Our title promises a doha a day, so we'll take them one at a time, slowly. Here's today's. It begins, in Hindi, bura jo dekhan main chala. In English, roughly: I went out looking for the bad one, and I couldn't find anyone. Then I searched my own heart, and found no one worse than me. Two lines. Notice the trick in them. The first line starts out on a hunt, a familiar one. Who's the problem in this office, this family, this group chat? The doha lets you go out looking, and then says, flatly: found nobody. And the second line turns the lamp around. It doesn't say you're terrible. It says the search only works in one direction, inward, and that's where the material is. This is Kabir's way. He doesn't argue. He sets a little trap in two lines, and the listener walks into it and springs it. Later, when the hunt for someone to blame starts up again, the second line can come back by itself. That's what a doha is for.
screen: `A WEAVER OF KASHI.` · `THE DOHA: TWO LINES THAT RHYME.` · `I WENT LOOKING FOR THE BAD ONE.` · then, large: `I SEARCHED MY OWN HEART.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one person you've been quietly blaming lately, for a mess, a mood, a delay. Let the case against them come up, as it usually does. Then, gently, without any punishment, turn the lamp around. Ask: what did I bring to this? Not to take all the blame, just to see your own part as clearly as you saw theirs. Stay with whatever you find, without arguing. If you pray, you can hold what you found before God. The bell holds the time.
Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi whose dohas, two rhyming lines, set little traps. Today's: I went looking for the bad one, and searched my own heart.
Your line: I searched my own heart. Today, the next time you start the hunt for who's to blame, let the second line come back: I searched my own heart. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Kabir's dohas are sung and quoted by followers of the Kabir Panth, in Hindu devotional singing, and in everyday talk; his verses are also kept in the Guru Granth Sahib.

fork.setup: you're Kabir, a young weaver who wants a teacher. the teacher you want comes down the steps to the river before dawn. what do you do?
options: wait at his door and ask politely.
lie down on the steps in the dark.
fork.reveal: tradition says he lay on the steps, Ramananda stepped on him and cried Ram, Ram, and Kabir took those words as his teaching.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poem saying I'm the worst person alive.
what it means: the hunt for the bad one only works turned inward, so the doha turns the lamp around.
what a scholar hears: Kabir's verses come down through several collections that don't always agree, so a doha known everywhere may be missing from the oldest ones.

notes: The doha is paraphrased in English and only its opening words are given in Hindi transliteration, unquoted. Confirm the opening words (bura jo dekhan main chala) and that the paraphrase is fair.
The outline says 'one a day for a week' but the brief gives Kabir three days (921–923); the script says so plainly. The owner may want to adjust the title or the day count.
Birth and initiation stories (Niru and Nima, the pond, Ramananda's foot on the ghat steps) are framed as tradition. Confirm.

howItsDone mentions the Kabir Panth, Hindu devotional singing and the Guru Granth Sahib; a Keeper (and a Sikh reviewer) should confirm the phrasing. Kabir is honored by more than one community; the script tries not to claim him for any one.
Original left null: the doha's language (an old Hindi mix) would be better given by a Keeper than guessed.

Editor pass: dropped the spoken 'we have three days with Kabir' (it contradicted the title on air); changed 'We know that hunt' and 'the second line comes back by itself' so the narrator no longer tells the listener what goes on in their head.

Audit pass: trapdoor third floor replaced (it restated the teach) with a note on the fluid Kabir corpus (Bijak, Guru Granth Sahib, Rajasthani granthavalis differ). A Keeper may want to check whether bura jo dekhan appears in the early collections; the script itself attributes it to Kabir as popular tradition does. Ramananda's dates and Kabir's are debated by historians; the meeting is kept as 'tradition says'.
